content.title: COOKING MISTAKES THAT QUIETLY WRECK YOUR {{HEALTHY}} MEAL
facts: **Boiling broccoli** – This drains most of the vitamin C and sulforaphane straight into the water; steam it for 5 minutes instead to keep the nutrients in the floret, not the sink.
**Olive oil** – Heating extra virgin olive oil past its smoke point breaks it down and creates harsh compounds; save it for finishing dishes or low-heat cooking, and use avocado oil for high heat.
**Salting meat too late** – Adding salt only at the table means it never penetrates the fibers; salting 30-40 minutes before cooking helps it season evenly and stay juicier.
**Overcrowding the pan** – Too much food at once traps steam instead of browning, so vegetables end up soggy and lose their crisp texture and flavor compounds.
**Tomato sauce** – Cooking tomatoes actually increases available lycopene, so 'raw is always healthier' isn't true here; a light simmer with a splash of oil boosts absorption.
**Draining pasta water** – Tossing all of it out wastes the starchy liquid that helps sauces cling to noodles; save half a cup before draining for a smoother, richer texture.
**Cutting vegetables too early** – Prepping and storing chopped veggies hours ahead lets exposed surfaces lose water-soluble vitamins to oxidation and air.
**Microwaving in the wrong container** – Reheating in certain plastics can leach compounds into food, especially fatty leftovers; glass or ceramic is the safer bet.
**Skipping the resting step** – Cutting meat right off the heat lets all the juice run out onto the board; resting 5-10 minutes keeps it inside where it belongs.

content.caption:
A few of these are worth slowing down for. Take broccoli: boiling it isn't just 'less ideal,' the sulforaphane precursor compounds are water-soluble, so they literally dissolve out into the pot — steaming keeps that enzyme system intact so your body can actually convert it. With olive oil, the issue isn't the fat itself but heat stability: once it passes its smoke point, some of the beneficial polyphenols degrade and the oil starts forming compounds you don't want more of, which is why chefs treat it as a finishing oil rather than a frying one. And tomato sauce is the fun exception — cell walls break down with heat, which frees up lycopene that your body couldn't access from a raw tomato, so cooked actually beats raw here. Everyone's kitchen habits are a little different, so start with whichever one feels easiest to fix first.
